newsitem.title: FRANCE: Court orders Renault to call plant meeting.
newsitem.headline: Court orders Renault to call plant meeting.

text.p: The Court of Appeal here ruled on Wednesday that car maker Renault SA must call a meeting of its European works council representing employees before it can close its Vilvoorde plant in Belgium.
Renault had appealed against a previous ruling by a Nanterre court which said it had not followed the proper procedures in arriving at the controversial Vilvoorde closure decision.
The Nanterre court had been asked to give a ruling by the car maker's unions.
Renault had planned to close Vilvoorde, near Brussels, on July 31. The plant employs some 3,100 staff and the February 27 closure news sparked wide protest by Belgian car workers.
"It's the best ruling we could have got. Renault has to start all over again with the procedure. The date of July 31 does not exist anymore," said Georges Jacquemin of the CSC christian labour union.

Renault said in a statement that the court in Versailles "confirmed that there was no requirement for prior notice to be given to the Renault European Group Works Council to implement the closure of the Vilvoorde plant".
"However, the court of appeal deemed it necessary for the European Group Works Council to be reconvened to examine information on the reasons and repercussions of the closure," the statement said.
"Renault intends therefore to go ahead with the procedure concerning the closure of the Vilvoorde plant which continues to be an industrial and economic necessity," it said.

A spokesman said the European Group Works Council would be convened this month and the closure could still occur before July 31 -- the date initially given by the company when it announced the shutdown on February 27.
Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said in April that a slight delay in the closure was possible but the decision itself was irrevocable.
Renault said it decided to close Vilvoorde because it needed to slash its cost base and improve competitiveness.

Lionel Jospin, leader of the Socialist Party, said on Monday that if the left won the parliamentary election of May 25 and June 1, the government would be ready to try to obtain a reversal of the closure decision.

"As shareholder in Renault and member of the supervisory board, the state would demand that other solutions be considered, studied and prepared to solve the problems that could exist concerning the production costs at Vilvoorde," Jospin said.
The French government has a 46 percent stake in Renault.
Renault closed 1.63 percent lower at 138.70 francs at 1334 while the CAC-40 blue-chip index was down 0.33 percent.
